rationale: A wins because it keeps four clean, defensible lanes without wandering outside the supplied facts. Its strongest move is “Peloton is calling itself profitable. Its own numbers disagree.” because it turns the adjusted-EBITDA/net-loss tension into a real markets story. B has sharper reporter targeting, but “Peloton stopped selling bikes and started renting them” is a factual face-plant: the update says rental expanded, not that sales stopped. Invented facts in a headline are not seasoning; they are poison.
gaps_in_A: “How Peloton's new CEO manufactured its first profitable quarter in three years” leans hard on an unnamed CEO; the proof list admits the profile is not pitch-ready without the CEO’s name, availability, and actual cost-cutting mechanics.
A’s journalist shapes are good but sometimes stop at beat labels like “business reporter” or “retail or subscription-economy reporter” instead of naming clearer outlet types.
“Peloton is calling itself profitable” is directionally fair, but it should keep saying “adjusted profitable” so the net-loss caveat does not have to clean up the headline’s mess.
gaps_in_B: “Peloton stopped selling bikes and started renting them” invents a strategic reversal. The facts say Peloton expanded rental nationwide; they do not say it stopped selling bikes.
“$2,000+ upfront purchase” and “The $2,000 bike is now a monthly bill” bring in an unsupplied price point. Maybe true in the world, but not in this record.

“a bid for a customer who was never going to put a four-figure purchase on a card” is a plausible consumer-spending hypothesis, not a fact. B treats the imagined customer as if the company update supplied them.

B pads the rental story into two nearby angles: “hardware-to-subscription conversion” and “who now finds a Peloton affordable.” The second can survive, but only with customer data; otherwise it is the first angle wearing street clothes.
